title: From Farm to Table
hint: Beef, pork, lamb; dairy, free-range, organic, local; a carton of milk, a dozen eggs, much/many
why: food is something we talk about every day: shopping, cooking, eating out and choosing what to buy. English has different words for the animal and its meat, and many food words are uncountable, so we need a loaf of, a carton of and much or many to talk about amounts.
know: a carton of milk, a dozen eggs, a jar of honey
understand: many eggs, much milk; a few, a little
able: shop at a market or farm shop and ask for the right amount
explain where your food comes from: The eggs are free-range and the beef is local.
talk about the food you buy and cook at home
mistakes: How much eggs do we need?
I'd like a dozen of eggs.
There is a few cheese left.
warmup: Where do you usually buy food: a supermarket, a market, a small shop or a farm?
What did you eat yesterday? Which foods came from a farm?
Do you check where your food comes from? What labels do you look for?

vocab.note: For most farm animals, the meat has a different name. Many meat words came into English from French about a thousand years ago.
rows: bacon and eggs, a ham sandwich, pork chops
milk and food made from milk: cream, butter, cheese, yogurt
fruit, vegetables and other food from a farm (uncountable noun)
animals that can walk around outside, not kept in cages
grown without chemical sprays or artificial fertilisers
animals that eat grass, not mostly grain
from near here / growing at this time of year (in season)
a shop on a farm; a market where farmers sell their own food
We go to the farmers' market on Saturdays.
a farm where you pick the fruit yourself and pay by weight
a person (or shop) selling meat / bread / fruit and vegetables
I got the sausages from the butcher's.
a carton of / a bottle of
a carton of milk, a bottle of apple juice
a kilo of / a bag of
a kilo of potatoes, a bag of flour
a jar of / a pot of
a piece of / a slice of
a slice of ham, a piece of cheese
many, a few / much, a little
How many eggs? A few. How much milk? A little.

say: BUTCHer has the vowel of put, not but; dozen sounds like duzzen; loaf and loaves rhyme with go; PRODuce (food) has the stress at the start, but the verb is proDUCE.

exercises.title: What's on the plate?
exercises.intro: Match each meat to where it comes from. Tap a word, then tap its meaning.

items.why: Beef is meat from cows and bulls: roast beef, a beef burger.
Veal is meat from a calf, a young cow.
Pork is the general word for meat from a pig: pork chops, roast pork.

items.r: salty pig meat, often fried for breakfast
items.why: Bacon is salted meat from a pig, usually cut thin and fried: bacon and eggs.

items.r: pig meat from the leg, often in sandwiches
items.why: Ham comes from a pig's back leg. It is often eaten cold, in sandwiches.
Lamb is the young animal and also its meat: roast lamb.
Mutton is meat from an adult sheep. It has a stronger taste than lamb.
Venison is meat from a deer. It is a B2 word you may see on restaurant menus.

items.post: of milk on your way home?
items.why: Milk comes in a carton (or a bottle). A loaf is for bread.
Say a dozen eggs, with no of. (Dozens of eggs means many, many eggs.)
Cheese is uncountable here, so use how much.
Apples are countable (one apple, two apples), so use how many.

items.post: butter left, so we need to buy more.
items.why: Butter is uncountable, so use a little. A few is for countable nouns: a few eggs.

items.post: of bread at the farm shop.
items.why: Bread is uncountable. Count it with loaf: one loaf, two loaves (f changes to v).

items.pre: These eggs come from hens that walk around outside all day. They are
items.why: Free-range means the animals can go outside and move freely, not stay in cages.

items.post: in June, so they're cheap and full of flavour.
items.why: Fruit that is growing now is in season. Use the preposition in.

items.pre: Milk, butter, cheese and yogurt are all
items.why: Dairy products are milk and food made from milk.

items.pre: We bought some sausages and a chicken from the
items.why: A butcher sells meat. You can say the butcher or the butcher's (shop).

items.post: : the farmer doesn't use chemical sprays or artificial fertilisers.
items.why: Organic food is grown without chemical sprays or artificial fertilisers.
Produce means food from a farm, especially fruit and vegetables. It is uncountable.

items.post: of honey, please. The small one.
items.why: Honey and jam come in a jar: a glass container with a lid.

items.post: of carrots? The ones with the green leaves.
items.why: Carrots with their leaves, bananas and flowers come in a bunch.

items.pre: The cows on this farm eat only grass, so the beef is
items.why: Grass-fed animals eat grass, not mostly grain.

items.pre: On Saturday we went to a
items.post: farm and filled two baskets with strawberries.
items.why: At a pick-your-own farm (u-pick in North America) you pick the fruit yourself and pay for it.

items.answer: How much milk do we need for the pancakes?
items.why: How much + uncountable noun + do we need + for what?

items.answer: Could I have a loaf of brown bread?
items.why: Polite request: Could I have + amount (a loaf of) + adjective + noun?

items.answer: We buy our eggs from a local farm.
items.why: Subject + verb + object + from where: We buy our eggs from a local farm.

items.answer: There are only a few potatoes left.
items.why: Potatoes are countable: There are only a few potatoes left.

items.answer: My children love bacon and eggs for breakfast.
alt: For breakfast my children love bacon and eggs.
items.why: Subject + verb + object + for breakfast. Bacon and eggs is a fixed pair.

exercises.title: Reading
exercises.text:
Riverside Farmers' Market: a visitor's guide

The market is open every Saturday from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m., from May to October. Everything is grown or made within 100 kilometres of the city, so the food is local and seasonal.

Start at the Green Valley Dairy stall. They sell fresh milk in glass bottles, butter, yogurt and more than ten kinds of cheese. Ask for a free taste of the blue cheese!

Next to them, Hill Farm sells free-range eggs by the dozen or half dozen, and grass-fed beef and lamb. If you want pork sausages or bacon, visit the Martins' stall at the end of the row.

For fruit and vegetables, go to Orchard Lane. In June they have strawberries, and in September apples and pumpkins. Come early: the strawberries are usually gone by ten o'clock.

Don't forget the bakery van near the entrance. Their sourdough loaves are famous.

Bring your own bags. Most stallholders take cards, but a little cash is useful.
exercises.intro: Read the guide. Then type the missing word from the text, and press Check.

items.why: Paragraph 1: 'The market is open every Saturday from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m.'

items.ask: How far away is the food grown or made?
items.why: Paragraph 1: 'Everything is grown or made within 100 kilometres of the city.'
Paragraph 3: 'Hill Farm sells free-range eggs by the dozen or half dozen.'

items.ask: What should you do if you want strawberries?
items.why: Paragraph 4: 'Come early: the strawberries are usually gone by ten o'clock.'

items.ask: What is the bakery van famous for?
items.why: Paragraph 5: 'Their sourdough loaves are famous.'

exercises.title: Speaking
items: Describe a market or food shop you like. What does it sell, and why do you go there?
Is it important to you that food is local, organic or free-range? Is it worth paying more for it?
What is a typical dish from your country with meat or dairy in it? How do you make it, and how much of each thing do you need?
Have you ever picked your own fruit or bought food directly from a farmer? What was it like?

parts.rule:
Watch out

  • countable: one egg, two eggs; many, a few, How many?
  • uncountable: no plural; much, a little, How much? To count it, use an amount: a loaf of bread, a carton of milk
parts.intro: Can you count it? Sort the food words.

chips.why: One egg, two eggs: countable. How many eggs?
One carrot, a bunch of carrots: countable.
One apple, a few apples: countable.
Milk is uncountable: some milk, a carton of milk. Not milks.
Butter is uncountable: a little butter, a pack of butter.
Bread is uncountable: some bread, two loaves of bread. Not breads.
Honey is uncountable: a jar of honey.
Flour is uncountable: a bag of flour, a little flour.

items.q: Can you buy two breads at the bakery?
items.why: Bread is uncountable. Say two loaves of bread.

items.q: How many milk do we need?
items.why: Milk is uncountable, so use how much.

items.q: We had roast pig for Sunday lunch.
items.why: Pig is the animal. The meat is pork: roast pork.

items.q: I'd like half a dozen eggs, please.
items.why: Correct: half a dozen eggs means six eggs, with no of.

items.q: There are a little apples in the bowl.
items.why: Apples are countable, so use a few. A little is for uncountable nouns like butter.

teacher.purpose: help general learners talk about food from the farm: the meat words that differ from the animal (beef, pork, bacon, ham, lamb, mutton), shopping and label words (dairy, produce, free-range, organic, grass-fed, local, seasonal), and the grammar of amounts: countable and uncountable nouns with containers (a carton of, a loaf of, a dozen) and much / many, a few / a little.
teacher.before: bring (or show on screen) some real food packaging: an egg box, a milk carton, a bread bag, a honey jar. Labels like free-range or organic are a bonus. Or ask the student to photograph three things from their kitchen.
plan: The three warm-up questions. Listen for breads, milks, fruits and for animal names used as meat (We ate pig). Note them for later.

Start with the animal and meat table: test by asking “What do we call meat from a pig?” Then the shopping words with your packaging. Then the amounts table: hold up each item and ask “What is it? A carton of ...?”
Matching, then the amounts. In Exercise 2, ask “Can you count it?” before each answer.
Do one together and set the other for home.
The market guide. First ask: “Which stall would you visit first, and why?” Then the questions. Follow-up: make a shopping list for the market with amounts (a dozen eggs, a loaf of sourdough).
Questions 2 and 3 are the core. For question 3, ask for a short recipe with amounts: “How much flour? How many eggs?”
Exercise 7 Part A together; Part B at home.
pron: loaf /ləʊf/, loaves /ləʊvz/: f changes to v, like calf, calves in Lesson 1.
produce: noun /ˈprɒdjuːs/ (stress first: local PROduce), verb /prəˈdjuːs/ (farms proDUCE milk).
yogurt: UK /ˈjɒɡət/, North America /ˈjoʊɡərt/. Both are fine.
mutton /ˈmʌtn/, veal /viːl/, venison /ˈvenɪsn/: three syllables, stress on the first.
mistakes: Animal vs meat. A nice story for students: after 1066, French-speaking nobles ate the meat (bœuf, porc, mouton) and English-speaking farmers looked after the animals (cow, pig, sheep). So the meat words come from French.
lamb, chicken, turkey, duck are both the animal and the meat. fish too. Only the big farm animals have separate meat words.
bread, milk, cheese, butter, fruit, meat, food are normally uncountable: some bread, a piece of fruit. Cheeses and fruits exist, but mean different kinds (B2).
a dozen eggs, not a dozen of eggs. But dozens of eggs (= a lot). The same with a hundred people / hundreds of people.
organic: Spanish ecológico / biológico, German and French Bio. In English say organic, not ecological or biological.
free-range is about how animals live, not price: free does not mean no cost. Some students guess this.
uk_us: Both are on road signs in Canada.
a box / basket / quart of strawberries
Punnet is very British; say box if unsure.
A farm stand is often a small table or hut by the road.
adapt: Focus on beef, pork, bacon, ham, lamb; dairy, free-range, organic, local; a carton of, a dozen, a loaf of, a bag of; much/many.
Add mutton, venison, veal, grass-fed, seasonal, produce, a punnet of, a sprig of, a pinch of, and kinds: French cheeses, tropical fruits.
Role-play shopping at a market stall: ask for three things with the right amount and price.
Discuss: Is organic food worth the price? Should cities have more farmers' markets? Give reasons and examples.
prompts: A market or shop you like. Follow up: “What do you usually buy there?” “How much does a dozen eggs cost?” Listen for breads and a dozen of.
Local, organic or free-range? Follow up: “Would you pay twice as much for free-range eggs?” “How do you know the label is true?”
A typical dish. Ask for a mini recipe: “How much rice? How many onions?” This drives much / many, a little / a few naturally.
Picking your own fruit. Follow up: “How many kilos did you pick?” “Did you eat any while you were picking?” A light, happy topic.

bank.q: Could you buy a ___ of orange juice?
bank.why: Juice and milk come in a carton or a bottle.
Potatoes are countable, so use how many.

bank.q: We only have ___ flour, so we can't make two cakes.
bank.why: Flour is uncountable, so use a little.
Bacon, ham, pork and sausages come from pigs.
Veal is meat from a calf, a young cow.

bank.q: There's a ___ near our house where you can buy vegetables straight from the farmer.
bank.why: A farm shop is a shop on a farm that sells its own food.

bank.q: These tomatoes are ___: they were picked yesterday, ten kilometres away.
bank.why: Local food comes from near where you live.

bank.q: I need ___ eggs for this recipe: six, I think.
bank.why: Six eggs is half a dozen eggs, with no of.

bank.q: Meat from an adult sheep is called ___.
bank.why: Meat from an adult sheep is mutton. From a young sheep, it is lamb.

bank.q: Milk, cream and cheese are ___ products.
bank.why: Dairy products are milk and food made from milk.

bank.q: Can you get a ___ of bread from the bakery?
bank.why: Count bread with loaf: a loaf of bread.

bank.q: There aren't ___ strawberries left, only five or six.
bank.why: Strawberries are countable, so use many in a negative: not many.

bank.q: The ___ cut the beef into four thick steaks for us.
bank.why: A butcher is a person who sells and cuts meat.

bank.q: We bought three breads at the market.
bank.why: Bread is uncountable. Say three loaves of bread.

bank.q: How much cheese would you like?
bank.why: Correct: cheese is uncountable here, so how much.

bank.q: Our eggs come from free-range hens.
bank.why: Correct: free-range hens can walk around outside.

bank.q: I'd like a dozen of eggs, please.
bank.why: Say a dozen eggs, with no of.

bank.a: How much butter do we need for the cake?
bank.why: How much + uncountable noun + do we need + for what?

bank.a: The farm shop sells honey from its own bees.
bank.why: Subject + verb + object + from where: The farm shop sells honey from its own bees.

bank.a: We had roast lamb with potatoes on Sunday.
alt: On Sunday we had roast lamb with potatoes.
bank.why: Subject + verb + object + time: We had roast lamb with potatoes on Sunday.
